title: With Melania, We See Nothing
summary: “Do you ever think about death?” Brett Ratner asks Melania Trump, midway through the second and final episode of Melania: The Series (as opposed to Melania, the movie, or Melania, the memoir, or $Melania, the cryptocurrency). content:
“Do you ever think about death?” Brett Ratner asks Melania Trump, midway through the second and final episode of Melania: The Series (as opposed to Melania, the movie, or Melania, the memoir, or $Melania, the cryptocurrency). Melania—typing her name this many times in a row has given me a dizzying feeling of semantic satiation—is sitting on Air Force One, shot in tight focus, wearing a black jacket and a faint scowl. “Of course you think about it,” she replies, revealing teeth so white, they’re almost blue. “You just want to make sure that, you know, the family or my child are taken care of. Any minute, something can happen. It’s very in, um, it’s in the stars.” And with that, the question is dismissed, the specter of mortality diffused as rapidly as air from a popped balloon.

I can’t say I felt for Ratner, exactly, watching all one hour and 11 minutes of Melania: The Series, because if it weren’t for the allegations of sexual harassment and assault made against him in 2017 (allegations that he denies), he wouldn’t have been exiled to creative Siberia and I wouldn’t have spent multiple hours watching Melania (the Trump) gliding purposefully into the spa at Mar-a-Lago or describing the many exciting benefits that blockchain provides for her fan base. But I’ve spent enough time interviewing resistant subjects to recognize the desperation kicking in as he realizes he’s got nothing. “Have you ever slept in?” he asks at one point. (Not really.) “Do you ever take long walks?” (She doesn’t.) “Do you have a favorite book?” (It’s Melania, of course.)

All the while, the camera stays trained on his subject, her eyebrows penciled heavily in two straight lines as if to minimize any human expression she might otherwise convey. Much has been made of how stultifying Melania: The Series is as a televisual experience—how devoid of action! How recycled of content! How toadying in approach! But the series’ emptiness also feels illuminating, in a metatextual kind of way. Ratner gives us such relentless footage of Melania, posed and composed and airtight, that he brings the whole project of documentary filmmaking into disarray. What does it mean to watch someone for such prolonged periods of time and see nothing at all?

Every day, we are awash in images and clips—“We sleep and eat the image and pray to it and wear it too,” as Don DeLillo wrote in Mao II. (As if to offer proof, in one scene in Melania: The Series, an assistant director clambers out from behind the camera to show Melania a photo of everything his brother rescued from his house in Los Angeles before it burned down in the 2025 wildfires—his guitars and his MAGA hats.) The president is a booster of artificially generated imagery, which tends to suit his particular aesthetic: gaudy, emotionally staged, ideological. And the most dominant movie of the moment is a documentary, You Can See Everything, which, like Melania, manipulates the visual and aural language of film, but as anti-propaganda, to show us how profoundly untrustworthy it has been all along.

In that nearly three-hour movie, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, Elizabeth Holmes’s face, like Melania’s, absorbs the camera. Fielder moves in with the disgraced Theranos founder and her partner, Billy Evans, in the weeks before she goes to prison for fraud. Holmes seems to be under the impression that through what Evans calls “radical transparency” she can persuade Fielder, and the rest of us, of her innocence. And so, for a few weeks, a pair of the most practiced illusionists in American culture go head-to-head in her rented, wood-paneled beach house: the Silicon Valley saleswoman and the comedian so committed to the bit that he once trained for almost two and a half years to become a commercial pilot, in service of his TV show. Two manipulators, each alike in proficiency. The question seems to be less about which one will prevail—Fielder has the lopsided power of final cut—than about whether anything unexpected will be revealed in the process.

From the beginning, Fielder and Oppenheim use angles and lighting to set up stock roles: Holmes, the mother clutching an infant, awash in natural light, is the heroine; Fielder, lurking in the darkness and grimacing, is her antagonist. Her face is almost ludicrously likable on camera, rubberized and wide-eyed, guileless, and the movie zooms in on it well past the point of discomfort. Holmes weeps, she breaks down, she locks eyes with Fielder so intently that the pair seem to be glued to each other. All this looking gives Fielder no insight into what to make of her, so in the second half of the film, after she goes to jail, he restages scenes of their meetings and even seeks the help of a professional actor to try to get inside her head.

None of it really works. Holmes remains unknowable, much as Melania does, despite all the time we’ve spent watching her, despite the “equivocal magic” of the image, as Susan Sontag once wrote, and despite the fact that You Can See Everything uses scenes and images to provoke every emotional response in the handbook: shock (unexpected full-frontal nudity), pathos (a devastated Holmes being led into prison), suspense (Hitchcockian angles and shadows). The score, by Ari Balouzian, all jagged strings and low, discordant humming, similarly seems intent on trying to make us feel.

For all of its prolonged run time, the movie is riveting. But it also clearly lays its tricks on the table: Storytelling is a fundamentally manipulative process, Fielder seems to argue by the end. Ratner uses many of the same techniques as Fielder to elicit emotion in Melania—heavy-handed aural hooks, close-ups, shameless scenes of devastation. He comes up short, but perhaps that’s because he lacks the true skill of canny scammers and filmmakers: sensing what people, in all our glorious and idiotic humanity, really want to see.

title: Here Comes Santa Claude
summary: When Cynthia Bell McGillis needs help with her holiday shopping, she turns to Mrs. Claus. Not the one in the North Pole, but her own custom-built AI agent. content:
When Cynthia Bell McGillis needs help with her holiday shopping, she turns to Mrs. Claus. Not the one in the North Pole, but her own custom-built AI agent. After getting a head start on buying Christmas presents last month, McGillis had an idea of how to more easily keep track of her purchases: “I bet Grok can help with that,” McGillis, who works in marketing for an AI start-up in San Diego, told me. She instructed Grok Bot, an AI assistant made by Elon Musk, to constantly scan her email inbox every day. “Mrs. Claus” now logs arriving items and who they are for, searches the newsletters McGillis subscribes to for sales on potential gift ideas, and keeps a running total of how much McGillis has spent. The day we spoke, the bot had just surfaced a discount on Old Navy Christmas-themed pajamas.

In recent months, tech companies have launched a number of AI personal assistants, one after the other. Instinct, an agent that allows users to chat with it directly from the iMessage app, went viral in August; the next month, Meta launched its competitor, Muse. According to Mark Zuckerberg, more than 10 million users tried Muse in its first six weeks. Unlike traditional chatbots, AI agents can act on your behalf in the real world: Feed them your credit-card information and online passwords (if you dare), and they can find restaurant reservations, book flights, and, yes, buy gifts on your behalf. This month, OpenAI debuted ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its agents to also make purchases for users.

[Read: AI agents are here. Nobody’s ready.]

Now, for the first time, some people are about to open presents that were chosen and purchased entirely by bots. When Rohit Bakshi, an AI-product director in the Bay Area, wanted to get his nephew a Tin Can, the popular Wi-Fi-enabled “landline” for kids, he messaged Instinct to buy it. Bakshi told me that using Instinct more for holiday shopping would be a “no-brainer.” I heard similar enthusiasm from Boaz Sobrado, a tech worker also based in the Bay Area. (Every agentic-AI-loving shopper I could find had some connection to the tech industry.) Sobrado recently asked his girlfriend’s Muse agent, which knows her Instagram likes and saved posts, to find a hotel that matched her tastes. Agents can crawl through hundreds of text messages and emails to identify a tailored gift—something the intended recipient mentioned a long time ago, maybe, or something they might like based on contextual clues.

AI companies are certainly invested in the notion that their personal assistants can be heroes this holiday season. In an email, Ben Schwerin, the chief business officer of Instinct, told me that the company has seen a recent uptick in people using its agents to shop. “What’s been interesting is people are trusting Instinct to complete purchases for a full gift list, rather than handing Instinct one-off links,” he said. Meanwhile, Meta is partnering with social-media influencers to tout how Muse can be used for holiday shopping, such as by choosing gifts on a budget. (Meta declined to answer questions about how people are using Muse for holiday shopping.)

Americans without ties to the tech industry so far seem less bought in. AI assistants, for the most part, have yet to fully enter the mainstream. Some of that gap may be principled: Much of the country, after all, remains concerned about AI’s rapid development, and people certainly have good reason to be uncomfortable with the idea of a bot shopping with their credit card and having detailed access to their family’s personal information. AI assistants can also be expensive, many requiring subscriptions that run more than $100 a month. Some major retailers, including Amazon, have banned AI agents; the e-commerce giant is reportedly worried about what shopping bots could mean for its advertising business.

Still, it may be only a matter of time. The promise of convenience can be hard to ignore. Lots of people who aren’t using agents to shop on their behalf are still asking AI for gift-giving help. This year, 40 percent of shoppers say they plan to use generative AI for holiday shopping, such as by asking ChatGPT for product recommendations, according to a recent report from Accenture. Kath Gramling, who leads the consumer-goods-and-retail division at Accenture, believes that many people who use LLMs may soon adopt AI agents too. “It’s just a natural extension,” Gramling told me.

More shoppers may soon experience what can go wrong when you let an AI personal assistant run wild. One man claimed on X that his AI agent accidentally posted his bank-account balances in a Slack channel at his workplace; another man told Business Insider that a request for ingredients to make dinner for two resulted in a 20-pound chicken-wing order. Indeed, not all of Sobrado’s purchases have been successful: He recently ordered flowers for his girlfriend using his Muse agent, which he named Hermenegildo. When the flowers arrived, he realized that the agent had attached a card for his girlfriend and signed it, With love, Hermenegildo.

[Read: It’s all fun and games until you give AI your credit card]

Even if you aren’t using an AI personal assistant to buy any gifts, the bots might still affect your holiday-shopping experience. Last month, a Verge reporter wrote that she was able to instruct her Muse agent to continuously hold items in her cart on the RealReal, blocking other potential shoppers from purchasing them on the secondhand-luxury-fashion website. (Following the report, the RealReal said that the company would make it more difficult for agents to shop on its website.) And yesterday, Walmart announced that the company will now let Muse agents browse for deals and make purchases on users’ behalf. Black Fridays of decades past were an endurance game of who could wake up at the crack of dawn and brave the freezing weather in pursuit of a deal. This Black Friday might be a competition of who has the best AI agent.

All of this raises the age-old holiday question: What is gift giving really for? AI agents will never be able to replicate the experiential aspects of holiday magic. I love spending weeks clicking through websites until I feel the eureka moment of finding the perfect gift that I know someone will love. Others enjoy walking in a physical mall during the holidays, past the twinkling lights and smiling Santa. Bakshi told me that he can’t imagine letting Instinct do all of his holiday shopping. “I like going to the stores,” he said. “There’s a lot of festivity to it.”

The principle stands that a Christmas gift is supposed to symbolize the love and appreciation you feel for a recipient. Instead, gift-giving frequently becomes a matter of commercialism and obligation. Now AI agents are opening the possibility of delivering incredibly personal gifts with about the same effort it takes to purchase a gift card. Hopefully for gift givers, they’ll get everyone’s name right.

title: How Did Any Child Survive the 1970s?

content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube

In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show, The Atlantic’s David Frum is joined by the author and journalist Meghan Cox Gurdon to discuss her new memoir, Free Range Girl, about growing up in the 1970s. They explore how parenting has changed, the risks and rewards of childhood freedom, and why the past may not deserve our rose-colored nostalgia.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Meghan Cox Gurdon: I would say that parents today would be arrested for half the things—for almost anything that we were allowed to do. I mean, it is quite extraordinary. The social norms were so different back in the day.

[Music]

David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. And for this Thanksgiving edition of The David Frum Show, I’ll be talking to Meghan Cox Gurdon, author of a new memoir of growing up in the 1970s, Free Range Girl. At the end of the show, I’ll offer some personal words of thanks to you, the viewers and listeners of The David Frum Show.

But before either the conclusion thanks or the dialogue, I want to talk at the beginning about why I invited Meghan Cox Gurdon to come and discuss her memoir of life in the 1970s.

I was inspired by a 2026 poll conducted by NBC News that found that nearly half of adults ages 18 to 29 said that, if they had the option, they would choose to live in the past. They didn’t mean the ancient past. They didn’t mean horse-and-buggy days. They meant the recent past: the 1970s or the 1990s, about which they have all kinds of nostalgic feelings.

So I wanted to tell them: I was there, and while definitely, like, the dating apps are making things worse and social media is a nuisance and AI is a little menacing, you do not wish you were there. You just don’t remember.

I remember during the birther controversy of the Obama years when people had this fantasy that President Obama was born in Kenya. Remember that? Now, we know that President Obama’s mother was present in Hawaii, attending school, in the spring of the year that he was born, 1961. The theory of the case was that she somehow got from Hawaii to Kenya to give birth to the president and came back. But I took my first airplane flight in the middle 1960s with my parents, and I can remember some of those flights. I just want to conjure up what it would have been like for the young mother of President Obama to do this.

I imagine a travel agent saying to her: Very well, Ms. Dunham, here’s your ticket. Honolulu to Los Angeles; Los Angeles to New York; New York to London; London to Nairobi. The Honolulu–Los Angeles leg of the trip by itself—and I looked this up—will cost more than a semester’s tuition at the University of Hawaii. You’ll have to pay by cash or certified check, since it’s exceedingly unlikely you qualify for American Express or Diners Club, as no other credit card yet exists. Bring plenty to read, since the in-flight movie has also only just been invented. I see you’re nine months pregnant, so you might ask the stewardess to seat you beside a passenger who doesn’t smoke. I hope your life insurance is up to date, since the risk of passenger fatality per mile is nearly 1,000 times greater than it will be in 2026.

I mean, what were they thinking? How would that be? But they don’t remember. They don’t remember the world before seat belts. They don’t remember the world of universal smoking. I don’t even understand quite how any of us who were children in the 1960s and ’70s got out alive. One of the defining experiences of our childhoods was riding in a front seat beside an adult, and when a car in front of you braked, the adult would fling out an arm. (Laughs.) As if somehow their arm would stop you from crashing into the hard metal headboard that would otherwise bash you in.

The past is a fascinating place. It’s full of interesting things to study. But you really don’t want to live there, and Meghan Gurdon and I will discuss why not in the segment that we’re about to begin.

[Music]

Frum: In 1976, the year America turned 200, a 12-year-old girl left her mother’s home in New York and moved to rural Maine to live with her father. He was a back-to-the-land man, and he had built the house himself. There was no hot water. The little girl bathed in a tin tub and carried spring water in by the bucket to heat on the stove.

That year, the girl rode horses bareback, and one of them threw her. She was found face down in a field with a concussion and two black eyes. She burned her eyebrows off lighting an oven while babysitting her little cousin. The girl was Meghan Cox Gurdon. She grew up to become a foreign correspondent, and since 2005 she has been the children’s book critic of The Wall Street Journal. She is the author of The Enchanted Hour, about why reading aloud matters. Her new book is the story of that year in Maine in 1976. It’s called Free Range Girl.

The book is about freedom, and also about what freedom costs; a childhood without screens or supervision among adults who are often busy with their own lives.

We hear a lot of arguments about how today’s children are raised. Meghan has lived on both sides of that argument—first as the child in the story, and then as the parent of five children herself. Meghan, welcome to the show.

Meghan Cox Gurdon: Thank you, David. I’m delighted to be with you.

Frum: All right, so let’s start with the story of that year in 1976. Tell us what you left, what you went to, and how it happened.

Gurdon: Well, actually, this is one of the interesting mysteries when you go back into the past to interrogate what happened, and when and why. It’s often quite difficult to put the puzzle pieces together. So in Free Range Girl, what I have done is I have represented what I understood at the time to be the case.

So I had been living with my mother in a variety of towns and villages around upstate New York and Western Massachusetts since my parents divorced in 1970. And we often had housemates—it was a kind of improvisational, 1970s nomadic sort of childhood with a single mother. And in 1976, my father had moved back to the land up in Maine perhaps a year or so earlier, and it was announced to me that I would be going to live with him for the next year.

And now, why that was—I think it’s not necessarily a known thing. But at the time I was told that it was so that I could get to know my father better. And in the way of children, I took the explanation that was given to me, and off I went. I packed my things up, including my bicentennial quarters, you know? Oh, because we had special bicentennial issues of everything back then. And I packed them all up into boxes, put them into the back of my father’s van, and he drove me up to Maine, which at the time seemed beyond everything. Like, you got across the border from New Hampshire into Maine, and it was like civilization ended. And that wasn’t true, of course; it’s a highly civilized place. But it seemed that way. Lots of trees, a lot of silence, not a lot of lights, not a lot of buildings. And that was my new reality.

Frum: We belong to the generation of parents who kept a very close eye on our children, and I think it’s a little hard for those who are any younger than us to remember just how little attention was paid to children of our generation who grew up in the 1970s.

You tell this story in a kind of very direct way, as you say. You tell what the child knew, not what the adult knows. But how unsupervised were you? How free-ranging were children allowed to be in the 1970s?

Gurdon: Well, I would say that parents today would be arrested for half the things—for almost anything that we were allowed to do. I mean, it is quite extraordinary. The social norms were so different back in the day that you didn’t even have to—in 1976, you didn’t have to wear a seat belt. The whole world was less security-oriented, less safety-oriented, so all of childhood was less safety-oriented. You didn’t wear a helmet when you rode bikes, necessarily. You certainly didn’t when, in my case, when you were riding on horseback. People didn’t wear helmets when they were skiing. It was just a completely different, less safety-oriented time.

And as a child, you were both given immense freedom to make mistakes. And, for example, you alluded to the blowing off of my eyebrows and eyelashes. That was when I had misunderstood how a gas stove worked. It was not a fatal injury. It was quite a useful injury in some ways. And I do think I agree with people like Jonathan Haidt who say that a certain amount of adversity in childhood does actually develop a child to be more resilient. It’s almost a meme now in the culture that if you grew up in our generation, you just kind of take things, you just sort of roll with it, and younger people are encouraged to be more fragile. And that’s regrettable, but the world has changed a lot.

Frum: I remember I attended what Canadians call junior high school, what Americans know as middle school: [grades] seven, eight, and nine. And at my junior high school, middle school—so these are children who are 13, 14, 15, not even 16—there was a teachers’ parking lot. And just next door to it, there was this big hydroelectric box, a relay station, which was just off, was on the province’s land; not on the school’s land. And the 13-, 14-, 15-year-olds would go to the box and smoke cigarettes. And because the school’s view is once you are off school property and onto some other level of government’s property—and it wasn’t illegal for 13-, 14-, and 15-year-olds to smoke cigarettes—and the school would do nothing, and there’d be a crowd of kids standing around the green box smoking cigarettes, and no one thought anything of it. And the parents who could see it, because they would come to the teachers’ parking lot to pick up the kids, they would see that it was just, No, that’s where the smokers stood.

Gurdon: So okay, so perhaps we today really look askance at smoking, and certainly smoking among the young.

But there is a kind of experimental quality to that age, anyway. And one of the things I think that really helped us as young people was that we were sort of allowed—we were given a little running room to experiment long enough to have some real-world reactions to things. Smoking—okay, the analogy doesn’t go that far, but if you think about, like, climbing things and falling off them, if you fell at the park—I wasn’t ever taken to parks because that involved too much probably parental involvement. But I gather, at school, you fall off the monkey bars. They were these metal bars, and you fell off them onto asphalt. You learned how to hang on.

And in fact, the epitaph for Free Range Girl comes from Charlotte’s Web. There’s a wonderful scene in Charlotte’s Web where E. B. White is writing about the Zuckermans’ barn. I don’t know if you remember this scene. But the Zuckermans’ barn is where Charlotte the spider and Wilbur the pig live, and this little girl, Fern, and her brother are on the swing. And E. B. White writes: Mothers from miles around feared that swing in Zuckerman’s barn. It’s just one of these enormous swinging things. And here’s the epitaph: But children always hold on more tightly than their parents think they will.

And I think that’s something that we have forgotten. I think that is something that subsequent generations of parents have forgotten—that children do hold on more tightly. If you fall off the monkey bars, you hold on more tightly next time. If you blunder in one way or another, you learn. You become less fragile. You learn from adversity.

Frum: So I have a number of things I want to go through with you. I want to start with the writing of the book, then about your experiences, and then to talk about this dialogue between the ages, then and now.

So let’s start with the writing. You, the human being who wrote the book, know the 50 years of history since 1976. But you, the author of the book and the character in the book, know a lot less than you, the human being. So how did you purge all the things you know about the adult world, about humanity—first as an author and then as a character? How did you roll it back?

Gurdon: I, actually, I would say I spent probably the first year that I was working on the book just working on it in my head, just trying to think. I was trying to decide: Should it be present tense, past tense? Should it be first person or third person? Should I put in gory details or leave out the gory details? Should I explain how things worked that were commonplace at the time and now unheard of, like a party line, you know? Eventually we got phone service at my father’s homestead, and we had a party line. Now, people of my generation know what that is, but people of, let’s say, who were born yesterday are not necessarily going to know what an artifact like that is. So—

Frum: What is it?

Gurdon: What is a party line? Oh, it’s—you don’t have a single dedicated phone line off your property. So you have a phone line that is shared with your neighbors or other parties. And so what would happen is, if you wanted to make a local call, you would pick up the receiver. And if you heard a dial tone, then you could call the local call, and if you heard voices, that meant that somebody else already had dibs on the phone line. And you would wait. It was not considered impolite, you know, to check maybe 30 seconds or a minute later, you know? And people who were having the conversation on the party line, the parties on that line, they would experience a little click—and they could kinda hear a hollow sort of sound that would tell them that some neighbor was trying to phone out. And that was for local calls. I mean, it’s so far away now. These were phones that were attached to the wall, an immovable object.

Also, if you wanted to make a long-distance call—this again was from rural Maine, and maybe not the case everywhere in the country in 1976—you had to dial an operator in a nearby town, and the operator would connect you to your party. And there was no voicemail. You couldn’t leave a message. So if you just got a ringing tone on the other end, you had to call back later. I mean, it was just far away.

Anyway, so, to go all the way back, so these are some of the questions that I was noodling over. And I would say it took me about a year to think about how I was going to approach it and also which stories to include, and what should the timeline be? Should it be the course of a single year, you know, 12 months of a single year? Should it be 12 chapters? How do you do it? Should it take place over several years? So at the end of all of that cogitation was the decision that I made to write the book in the third person, and my goal here was to just to try and capture what it was like back then.

And yeah; so I wrote it in the third person, and that allowed me to get a little bit of kind of storytelling distance. It was more like I had the idea, maybe it would be something that would be very digestible for young people to read. I wasn’t exactly writing for a young audience. I was more writing something that could be read by young people as well as older people. So creating a time capsule that would be accessible to others.

And then later on in the process, the pressure came from outside; my agent and my husband and various other people said, You know, you should really think about putting this in the first person. So it went from me writing about myself, Meg, a character, to writing the I: I did this, I did that. You know, and the remove of time is sufficient that I—the whatever I am, woman in her early 60s, you know, 50 years away from the events of I, the 12-year-old—I mean, every cell in my body I think has been replaced since then. So I’m like George Washington’s axe, you know? Is any part of me actually the person who was there? Yeah, memory, I guess; that part of me is there.

Frum: Well, I talked about this dialogue between the girl in the book, the author inside the book, the author outside the book.

There’s another dialogue that I think—and this, I think, will be the power of the book to people who don’t remember our generation. There’s a dialogue between the girl in the book and what she thinks is okay and normal. The author, you, outside the book, and your idea of what is okay and normal, which is pretty robust. And the child takes everything for granted. You, the author, have a pretty robust view, and then many of the readers of this book will say, “Good God, that went on in 1970?”

Gurdon: (Laughs.) I know.

Frum: That’s how? How did Mom or Gra—how did they live to see this day? I look back on the period and think, How did anybody escape that period alive?

Gurdon: As a 12-year-old—and maybe this is true of all children through all time, I don’t know—but the things I was; I was a bit of a scaredy-cat, I think, actually. There were things that frightened me. I was very worried, for instance, about vampires. I had a very serious fear of vampires. Which I, of course, fed by reading vampire books like Stephen King’s Salem’s Lot and Dracula itself, the original book. Fun fact: By the way, the front cover of Free Range Girl shows a little cottage or a little house in the woods in wintertime, and there’s smoke coming up from it, and there are words in the smoke. Those words come from Bram Stoker’s Dracula, because it really exerted this huge power on me.

Anyway, I was afraid of vampires. I was afraid of grizzly bears, which do not exist in Maine. I was afraid of spiders. I was afraid—my cousin and I found a severed pig’s head in the woods, and we were afraid of that. I was afraid it was going to get me.

Frum: That is pretty scary.

Gurdon: But the things that actually, you know, now as a parent or grandparent as I am now, the things that actually represent a menace to a child of that age—like strangers, or going bareback without a helmet on a 16-hand-high horse at high speeds, riding the Greyhound bus by myself between Maine and Boston. Or even parental divorce. Which represent—and, like, a sequence of boyfriends involved with my mother. Those things represent actual danger.

But the child of 1976 was far more worried about, you know, Barnabas Collins coming out of the shadows.

Frum: Right. Well, the great thing about vampires was they obeyed very rigid rules. They couldn’t come in your house unless you somehow were tricked into giving them permission.

Gurdon: That’s right.

That’s true. I mean, you’re absolutely right, but I’m not sure as a 12-year-old that I was kind of really alive to the possibility that I could protect myself.

So, at the point at which I was most afraid of being intercepted by a vampire. Which is, again, one of these things that just—I mean, lots of people have grown up in rough ways one way or another. When I would have to tiptoe out to the outhouse in the dark, and then I was terrified that a vampire—I would be sitting there in the dark, vulnerable, and the door would fly open, and a vampire would be standing there. I mean, there’s some sublimated weirdness here. But a vampire would be standing outside, with his cape rippling in the moonlight, and then he’d get me. That was probably my most intense fear at the time.

It was—I mean, it was a lot to adapt to. Also, you know, going from flush toilets and hot and cold running water that just came out of the wall—you would just turn a tap and it would just come out—to an entirely different world where nothing was automatic. I mean, to heat water—as you mentioned at the beginning—to heat water, the wood had to be chopped and stacked and dried, and then it had to be carried into the kitchen. And we had two mechanisms for burning wood. One was a heat stove, which was used in the winter always, and there was also a cook stove, which was used even in the summer. Which was really, I mean, it was like something from Little House on the Prairie. It was this beautiful cast-iron thing with a little firebox on the left. And in order to, you know, heat water, you, again, did not turn a tap in the wall. You had to haul water from the spring in a bucket, and put it on the stove, in a vessel of some kind having started a fire in the firebox.

And it was laborious, and it was kind of absurd in a way. I mean, you didn’t, we didn’t have to live this way. You know, in the 19th century you did, but by the 20th century you really didn’t. It was partly an expression of my father’s romanticism. I think he really admired that way of that sort of self-sufficient life, of Thoreau and people of that ilk.

But it was also—there was a lot of tactile pleasure in it. And one of the things I really wanted to capture when I started writing Free Range Girl is how very different the world was when you had physical feedback from almost everything all the time. We are accustomed to, habituated now, to these smooth movements—smooth surfaces interfacing infinitesimally fast. Actually, that’s the wrong term, but you know what I mean. Like, so quickly; there’s no delay with anything that we want. We can swipe right, we can swipe left, we can swipe up, we can scroll. And it just wasn’t like that then. Everything had a knob. Everything had a switch, or it had an actual latch that you had to unlift.

So there were compensations for the peculiar primitive nature of it all.

Frum: This wasn’t Little House on the Prairie, which is—your choice was living in a tenement in a city and being a manual worker or having some land of your own and still being a manual worker, but at least owning the fruits of your labor, and so that was attractive.

These are people who—you could live in Boston and have hot water instantly, and you choose not to. And one of the things I look back on is to say: How do we explain the adults of 1975 and ’76 who are so, by our contemporary standards, so neglectful? So heedless of the dangers that their children were incurring?

Gurdon: Okay, so just this morning, knowing I was going to talk with you, I was thinking a little bit about this. One of the things that Free Range Girl has done, one of its effects that I was hoping it would do, is it causes people who read it to reflect on their own childhoods. And I’ve been hearing extraordinary stories from friends of mine.

So I would say—so here I am, divorced parents kind of living for themselves, and I’m sort of tagging along, fitting in. But there were parents who adhered to the old script, who stayed married, who maybe prioritized the cocktail hour and getting dressed and going to the country club and whatever. And they, too—there was a kind of neglectful fecklessness about those people, too.

I heard an extraordinary story this weekend from a friend of mine who said that her parents—you know, they had stayed married. They were very organized. They lived in comfort in Chicago. And they were having a cocktail party one night, and something caught on fire in the kitchen. And so the fire department was called, and everybody was hustled out of the apartment. And one of the firemen said to my friend’s mother, she said, the fireman said, Is there anyone else in the apartment? And she said, Just the cat. Totally forgetting her two daughters who had been put to sleep in the bedroom.

So, I don’t think it was just the back-to-the-landers who were, who just—I know you’ve written about the ’70s extensively. There was a kind of real prioritization of “me”—me being the self-actualizing adult. So the adult might think, I want to live a glamorous life and, you know, have cocktail parties. And that was valorized and allowed. Or the adult might say, I want to be freed from the constraints of marriage. I want to really experience my independence, my intellect, my sexual autonomy, whatever. And they also misbehaved with regards to children.

Frum: Alcohol was a factor back then, too, in a way that’s very hard for people who live a kind of normal bourgeois life to imagine today. About how—that woman who forgot the two kids. You put yourself in that situation; you think, Oh, how, how could she forget? Well, she probably had more drinks in that evening than her counterpart today would have in a week.

Gurdon: Right. And also cigarettes, remember? Of course, they don’t addle the mind quite so much. But do you remember back in the day, it was just everything smelled like cigarettes all the time. And every place you went, there were cigarettes; there were ashtrays. There were ashtrays in cars. There were, as you had experienced at school, there was a completely acceptable kind of middle-school smoking, behind-the-gym kind of thing.

We can’t celebrate that age too much. It’s very easy to look back with nostalgia, because when you’re young, the world is fresh and exciting, and those things seem very distinct. You know, was it more fun for parents? Possibly. Maybe.

Frum: Well, you and I, I think, have slightly different views. I think you, because of your robust attitudes toward child-rearing—I look back on the age with total horror. I have no nostalgia. If I could send, if I could put United States Marshals in time machines and send them back in time, I would do so. That’s obviously not feasible.

But the one place where I have some sympathy—I’ve been writing about this; I’ve been working on a memoir for a while myself. And the one thing I’m looking back on that age where as we were just, as we know, everyone was—the adults were engaging in sexual autonomy and splitting up. My parents who stayed together until my mother’s death would say that they felt like the characters in the movie The Last Married Couple in America—well, they were in Canada. I mean, everybody was getting divorced, and they weren’t. And it’s almost like, What was wrong with you?

And I think back on it. So the people of my parents’ generation, I think yours: They were children during the Depression. They were too young for the war. But they were pulled as, I mean, there was this tremendous shortage of young people in the world of the 1950s. And so they were pulled, like, by this wind tunnel of advancing pressure into adulthood at an extraordinarily early age.

So people now say, Well, wow; back then, you know, by the time you were 30, you owned a house. Yeah, by the time you were 30, you owned a house, and you were married, and you had kids, and they’re six and seven years old. And then you suddenly were 30, and you had married this person at, if you’re a woman, at 19, 20, 21. If you’re a man, at 23, 24, 25. You had two kids, maybe three under the age of 10. You did own a house, but you had a mortgage. You were in a job, and you were a full-blown adult at age 32. And you thought, Where was my youth?

Gurdon: And then you suddenly have a culture springing up, of liberation springing up around you. Or what was called liberation, probably about as—

Frum: And one more thing, which is, so if you are our parents—my father was born in 1931, and my mother was born in 1937. Nobody’s born in those years. I mean, it was the Depression. Then suddenly—so now you’re 32, and the world is full of all of these 20-somethings born in 1946, ’47, ’48, ’49, ’50, ’51. Young people of the opposite sex, very footloose, who are having a youth. And you think, Why did God decide that I was going to be a junior partner in an accounting firm at age 32, with a house, yes, and kids—and there are all these young people around who are having much more fun than I was ever allowed to? Now is my turn. And those two kids of mine, they’re going to pay on the front end what I paid on, what I’m paying, to make up for what I lost on the front end.

Gurdon: Yeah, I think there was a lot of reassuring propaganda around children at that time. I think you’re being generous to the parents who were deciding to dissolve their marriages in their 30s and 40s at that time. And that they would imagine that their children were paying.

I think one of the great lies of the era was this notion that children would be better off, that everybody’s better off, if mother and father do not live together anymore. Mom will be happier, Dad will be happier, and kids will be happier too, because they’ll be in a conflict-free home, and they’ll see what authentic love is when their parents meet other people.

I mean, obviously, not every divorce was a catastrophe. I know of a number of divorces in which things worked out really beautifully. And so one can’t make a blanket statement. But I think for a lot of us—it was not myself, but others who have read Free Range Girl said, This is a divorce book, really.

And honestly, I wrote it. But as Tom Stoppard once said about his plays when people were finding leitmotifs in them, he said, Well, I can see that they’re there, but I didn’t put them in myself. It’s a little like that. I don’t think of myself as having written a divorce book, but it was all over childhood.

Frum: Let’s ourselves go through this veil of ignorance and do the exercise you did, and go back to that time—because you are making here an implicit case: We really have lost things. So what did Meg in the book have that a modern Meg might reasonably, and while keeping her eyebrows—

Gurdon: Yeah. (Laughs.)

Frum: Might wish she had?

Gurdon: You know, I think that there was an—you, as a child. I can speak only for myself here; obviously there are many types of children and people, and I was a kind of cheerfully oblivious bookworm. And I was an only child. Therefore, I didn’t share anything. I had no distractions. I had no other people, and I had an immense amount of free time. And the time was not merely free and unscheduled; it was also, it was sort of mentally, intellectually free. I simply didn’t have any cluttering in my head. And this is, I think, one of the greatest differences between then and now; that before the internet, there was simply no alternate reality.

Clearly, you could think about the past; you could think about the future; you could imagine yourself in a different place; you could imagine stories that you’d seen on movies or television or in a book or whatever. So to that degree, there has always been available to the human mind an alternate reality.

But what we have now is so profoundly different. And has changed us, I think, so much, that even when you are untethered from technology now, you are alive to the existence of technology a mere short distance away. You just go into the next room. I mean, it’s great that you and I can talk like this—thank you, technology—but it has also, I think, affected our ability to be in time the way that we used to be in time.

So that is something I think that Meg of the past really—I mean, this all sounds so clichéd, because everyone’s talking about it now, talking about childhood then and now. But it is really true that there are blessings in a skinned knee, and there is a blessing in downtime where you have to just be in your own head, and there’s no entertainment, and there’s nothing else around. There’s no other way for people to contact you. You’re just in the moment. And there was a kind of autonomy about this.

So I mentioned earlier about not wearing a helmet when I rode horseback. That is actually one of the things that shows the trade-offs to me, the loss and gain. So if you wear a helmet, you are a lot safer if you are thrown from your horse and your head hits the asphalt. I mean, no question. You might not go to the hospital for a week, as I did back in the day. But if you don’t wear a helmet, you have the whole sky over your head. You have all the birdsong in your ears. You feel the breeze stirring your hair. There’s a kind of aesthetic, natural pleasure that you get from being unprotected, that it’s obliterated if you are protected.

And I think we can extrapolate out from that in all kinds of directions. If you have to get yourself from point A to point B and no grown-up is going to drive you, then you’re walking on the side of the road, okay. You know, you could get hit by a car. Something bad could happen. Also, there’s the wind, there are the leaves, there are the flowers, there’s the crunch of the ground under your feet. So you’re getting a lot, as well as losing things.

Frum: One of the things I remember being struck by, especially with our youngest children when the smartphones began to circulate, was meeting kids of 10 and 11 years old who had no idea where they were, or how to get from where they were to a store five or six blocks away by themselves.

Gurdon: Yeah. Actually, my husband tells an amazing story. When he was seven, my husband’s father, my father-in-law, he was a little concerned that little Hugo wasn’t showing enough autonomy or whatever. I think he was mistaken, but anyway. So he got my husband, who was then seven, up out of bed in the morning, drove him a couple of miles away from where they lived, and made him get out of the car. He said, Find your way home. (Laughs.) Because he was concerned that his seven-year-old child would—so, you know, it’s a really interesting thing.

I mean, so okay, in the Laura Ingalls Wilder books, there’s a very bad boy. People who’ve read those books will remember this. He’s a child who—oh, Charlie, I think his name is—he will not obey his father. His father bosses him around, and the kid won’t obey. And you see in the story of Charlie in this particular book: So Charlie is misbehaving in the field, he’s supposed to be working. He’s gambling about, and he steps on a hornet’s nest, and he’s horribly stung, and it’s a great morality tale.

And I think that parents in the way-past were pretty careful to try and inculcate in their children a kind of obedience to voice commands for exactly that reason. Because there was a lot of danger out there. Or making sure that your children can find their way home. Like, what if he gets lost? Well, he’s got to find his way home. You’re right; those are skills, those things. Finding yourself in the universe and getting—

Frum: There was also, in your book and in my memory, there was no homework. This is something that I remember: the first time I encountered homework. I transitioned schools in the middle of 10th grade. I went to a kind of, it wasn’t exactly a pri—it was like a lab school. It was affiliated with the University of Toronto; it was in the public system, but outside the public rules. And it was the first time I’d ever encountered homework before. It was a shocking imposition that you would come home, that your time was not your own when you came home from school. And I cannot remember before 10th grade ever having homework.

And young Meg in the book, she doesn’t have any homework.

Gurdon: Oh, she does. There’s one incident; you might remember this. I was assigned a term paper. It was called a term paper, and it had—

Frum: Yes.

Gurdon: And it had footnotes. It was so exciting. But you know, I typed my term paper on an old Underwood typewriter that my grandfather had bought at a tag sale and refurbished. You really had to use a lot of finger strength to get those things to click, to click the letters.

But you’re right. Otherwise, there—you say imposition. That’s right. When you got home, you were in this other reality. You had just your, maybe your chores to do, maybe a local friend you would see. You were just basically on your own. You weren’t still working for school. You weren’t still accountable to people from school. There was no group chatting. There was no checking your Insta and your Finsta and any of that. That—speaking of impositions—is a real imposition on adolescents, young adolescents today. I mean, there’s a sense in which they have to serve the internet in order to fit in with their peer groups.

We didn’t have to do that.

Frum: And the adult certainly would never consider helping you with homework. It wouldn’t occur to anybody; it wouldn’t occur to the child to ask, or the adult to do.

Gurdon: No. I did make the mistake of asking my father for help with math once or twice. He was a very hot-tempered guy in those days, and he couldn’t—I’m one of those people for whom math only ever made sense, the thing we were learning only made sense when it was too late. Like the next week you would learn; I don’t know. Like, see, I don’t even know enough about math to explain what I didn’t know. But the scales would fall from my eyes a little too late to fix my grade. So I was always a little behind.

For instance, I did not, or no one told me, I just did not understand that division was the opposite of multiplication. So I made the mistake of asking my father a couple of times for help with math. And then I didn’t, because he got so cross with me for being such a dolt.

Frum: And then we became adults, and there we were helping our children to make models of Independence Hall or Windsor Castle or something out of Play-Doh or flour.

Gurdon: Yeah. Or the terrible thing where they would say to you, at 8 o’clock on a Sunday night: Oh, by the way, I need a tri-board and paint by tomorrow, ’cause I have to do a project for tomorrow morning about the weather. The cycle of rain and evaporation or whatever. And then you’d have to hustle out to the local drugstore and buy the tri-board. Tri-boards, we didn’t have tri-boards in 1976. Maybe we did. I had a deprived upbringing. There were probably children who were having a very deluxe time, and their mothers had to run out and get tri-boards at 8 o’clock on a Sunday, but not mine.

I mean, my parents wouldn’t even drive me anywhere. The idea that an adult would—as is customary today—that an adult would structure his or her day around the need to transport children at a time of the child’s convenience was, I would say, that was pretty much generally unheard of. Even parents who were more attentive to their children, children I knew back in the day—if you wanted to go to town for something, you wanted to go to the store for something, you kind of had to hitchhike along with some other adult, not even necessarily in your own household, who was going to go and do that thing.

And if you wanted to go to the store at 2 o’clock in the afternoon, but the ride was leaving at 1 o’lcock, you left at 1 o’clock. I mean, the idea that your convenience would come first, would supersede an adult’s convenience, was just—it was fantasy.

Frum: So how does this end for Meghan, the book? She is going to return to the city someday. How does that happen?

Gurdon: So I can’t tell you, because it would spoil the ending of the book. But I will say that at the ending of the book, after having had this experimental year in Maine, this poor little only child from a broken home has to make a big decision about where she’s going to live, and her decision is what ends the book.

And forgive me for being coy, but I hate to blow up the ending.

Frum: Then let me ask you to widen out the aperture and tell me the social ending. How does this world that you describe—when do you think that comes to an end? When do parents start driving children to things? I can’t remember my parents, for example, ever attending a sporting event or a school play, and they were reasonably attentive parents.

They’re—well, no, they weren’t attentive parents, but they were involved and caring and loving parents who stayed together. But they would’ve been shocked to be asked. I would never have asked, and no one else was there. But when does the world we know—where the parents, you know, the dress rehearsals, the parents are there? The soccer games, the parents are there. The chauffeur service begins. When does all of that get going, do you think?

Gurdon: Yeah. I mean, you know, David, you probably have demographic answers to this. What I see is there are some various cultural influences that produced this world.

One, there was a murder. It was really awful. A little boy in New York City, I think he was called Etan Patz, something like that, and he was a little guy, like six, seven years old. And it was his first day of school. And his mother, his parents agreed to let him walk a block to his school, and he never made it, and for many years his murder was unsolved. I think finally it was solved. But the death of that little child happened at the same time that we began to get 24-hour news.

And then with access to 24-hour news, there was also the press of the news cycle in the home, on every person. You’re aware of things happening around the world. I mean, we’re so accustomed now to being absolutely connected to all things—and to be able to find out at a moment’s notice anything happening in any remote part of the world—that it does seem like ancient history.

But there really was a time, and within living memory, when you would have to exert some effort to find out what was going on places. And therefore, so we had the growth of the 24-hour news—or the onslaught of 24-hour news—which needed to find material. If it bleeds, it leads, right? The old local-news saying. So I think that, I would call it the early ’80s is when things really began to shift.

Frum: Do you think it was also when that generation of child who was the Meg of the book becomes a parent himself or herself, and says: You know, kind of wish my parents had been at the soccer game. I’m going to go?

Gurdon: Yeah; I think that may be so. That may well be so. I mean, I myself may be an outlier on this. I really—I, of course I wanted to go to my, or I felt that I should go, to my children’s things. But I will say for myself—I started having children in the late ’90s. And we moved, my husband and I moved our family back to the United States in 2000. Well, North America. Call it in 2000, something. I don’t know exactly. And I felt at that time that I was stepping into a fully formed parenting culture, and I was out of step with parenting culture.

By 2000, parenting culture, it was very conciliatory. Children were given a lot of choices. Fathers would kneel down and say, How ya doing, buddy? to their children. You know, Okay, time to go. Okay, Daddy’s going to go to the car now. There was a real softening of parental authority, and there was also a great focus on what we now would call maxxing. So maxxing the nutrition value of the foods that your children ate; maxxing the time, the out-of-school extracurricular activities, you know.

Again, when did it happen? My guess is probably somewhere between 1980 and 2000. By the time I got there in 2000—I already had a couple kids at that point—what seemed to me a very repressive and strangely adult abnegating culture had very much taken hold.

Frum: Is there some way to capture what was liberating and free for Meg in the book while protecting the eyebrows, and head from concussion? Is there any way to get the best of—or are these just inevitable trade-offs? You have the freedom, and you have the danger; you have the safety, you don’t have the freedom. Can modern parents find some wisdom in the story of your book, to say—how do they get the best of this without the worst?

Gurdon: So this is a hard question to answer. I would recommend a tradition we had in our family, and our tradition was called, If you can climb it, you can climb it. In other words, if there were an imposing wall or very tall trees, if a child could get up into the tree or up onto the wall, then the child was allowed to go. But we were not going to help you get up. So occasionally a child would say, Oh, I want to climb this maple tree. Can you help me get up on the first branch? And my rule was, No, I will not help you get up on the first branch. You have to show the tenacity that you can get up onto that branch. But if you get up onto that branch, you can climb as high as you wanna go. I would let them do that.

Is that good advice? I don’t know. I do think that we suffocate children somewhat by preventing them from having adventures by themselves, taking risks by themselves, learning to hold on. You know, nagging them all the time: “Hold on. Don’t go too high.” You know, it’s such a bummer. Who wants to be told that all the time? It’s natural for children to try to seek, to strive, to learn from experience. You know, to get up on things. If even, if a roof can be got up onto, get up on the roof, you know? It’s—you could fall off, sure. But what you lose in preventing that kind of experimenting, it seems to me, is more than what you gain by preventing it.

Frum: And the eyebrows grew back?

Gurdon: The eyebrows grew. See, eyebrows grow back. Bones knit back together. Concussions—I don’t know if my concussion has given me lifelong problems. Probably. But also, it was a kind of, it was a big experience. And I think that it’s worth having.

You remember there’s that line from the movie Finding Nemo—which is all on this theme, of course, of a highly protective father who feels that his son needs to be shielded from adversity. And there’s another fish character who says to the fish father—this worried fish father, he says, I’ll never let anything happen to you, to his son. And the other fish says: Well, that’s not much fun for him, is it? And that’s pretty much where I come down on it.

Frum: The artless, in-the-moment way in which the book is written, that is actually your considered view of looking back on this time, and all the hazards, to say, You know what? The girl was right.

Gurdon: You know, that is a bit difficult. I don’t think that I do really think that. I wrote about the past as it really was—partly as a tonic for the way that things are now, and partly just to try and bottle what it was like. It was a way of life. It was a degree of neglect that was really quite remarkable. And things that I saw when I revisited the past that I had not noticed going by, I represented as seen by the child with, I hope, some truth.

There is, for example; you’ll remember, that winter of 1976 was very—there was a lot of snow, a lot of ice. It was a big, heavy winter in New England, and I didn’t have a winter coat. My father never thought to get me a winter coat. My mother, who was not living with me up in Maine and therefore not seeing me cold every morning, didn’t think to get me a winter coat. It simply didn’t occur to the adults who were in charge of me, and I was aware that money was tight, and so I just made do.

And so people would ask me—I had a windbreaker, and I put a vest over the windbreaker. And I had mittens, but they didn’t quite meet the windbreaker sleeve, and the windbreaker sleeve got burned, and it was all a little bit haphazard. And people would say to me, Oh, aren’t you cold? And I’d say, No, I’m fine. Well, you know; that’s not true. And I don’t recommend that way of life. I think that if you can get a winter coat for your child, you ought to do it.

So I’m not being prescriptive here. I’m being descriptive. I’m trying to be descriptive. I’m not so much condemning modern parenting and modern life as I am holding a mirror up to it.

Frum: Well, I will say as a reader of Free Range Girl in both the galley and the printed form, that the literary achievement is you burn away everything that the adult world might know. And you just—you make us all remember what it was like, how our memories were when we were children, and the world was fresh and new, and everything was taken for granted.

And just because it was the way it was, you couldn’t imagine any other way that it might be than the way it was. That all comes later. And just that direct immersive experience. And I think many people who read Free Range Girl will be prodded to think about their own childhood, whether it was in that era or a later era. And to say, just remembering how things were liberates you from the present. But remembering the present does cast some judgment on the past. (Laughs.) But maybe the past more than amply deserved, if one were a child.

Gurdon: Thank you. I think that’s right. And I mean, look—if the book gives readers a feeling that they have traveled a little in time, and if it causes them to reflect on their own childhoods, I would say mission accomplished right there. That is really what I was hoping to do.

Frum: Well, Meghan, thank you so much for this talk, and thank you for Free Range Girl. And every success with the book, and have a great Thanksgiving.

Gurdon: Thank you, David.

Frum: Bye-bye.

title: I’m Not Going to Play Grand Theft Auto VI
summary: As a member of the puritan third of Americans who do not play video games, I’ve been disoriented by the hoopla around the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, but also mesmerized by it. content:
As a member of the puritan third of Americans who do not play video games, I’ve been disoriented by the hoopla around the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, but also mesmerized by it. This is, I imagine, how it feels to be in a foreign country as it celebrates a national holiday you only dimly understand. People smile and make loud noises and engage in cheerful rituals that are as mysterious as they are, evidently, important.

From reading the extensive coverage of GTA 6—and hearing about the broader franchise over the years from acquaintances who play it—I do know this: Grand Theft Auto is a series of games in which players wander around replicas of various cities committing crimes, including robbing banks, stealing cars, selling drugs, and killing civilians and police officers. And this latest installment is, according to a swiftly building early consensus, very, very good.

[Read: ]Grand Theft Auto VI is really weird

Reviews of the game in both mainstream and gaming outlets have declared it a “masterpiece” that is at once a penetrating satire of American excess and a tender romance. Critics have noted in particular how much more mature GTA 6 is than previous iterations of the franchise, which debuted in 1997. Gone, for example, are the beddable (and killable) prostitutes—a controversial mainstay of the earlier games. Instead, players work to maintain a relationship between the protagonist, Jason, and his girlfriend, Lucia. As Jason, a player can hold hands with Lucia, paint and clean their house in preparation for her release from jail, and engage in pleasant mundanities such as grocery shopping. You can even lie in bed next to Lucia and doomscroll on your phone. “Much of what you can do—apart from activities routine to G.T.A. like stealing cars and robbing banks—is taking action to care for and nurture your romantic partner,” a New York Times reviewer wrote.

I don’t doubt that the game is, as its boosters claim, arresting and disarming in its opportunities for compassion. Perhaps it is even “high art,” as one review declared. But for all the praise GTA 6 is receiving, I’m not tempted to buy a console and join the gaming masses, and I can’t help but feel uneasy that legions of adults are spending their time and money on this spectacle.

For one thing, the game is still incredibly violent, despite its new focus on domesticity: The thieving, drug dealing, and innocent-bystander-murdering remain. One clip of the game, which shows a player conducting a mass shooting at a hospital, has been viewed more than 25 million times on X, in a thread that includes other in-game mass shootings at an airport, at a police station, and on a downtown street. Defenders of the franchise have claimed that this hyper-violence is the backbone of what is actually “a sharp, progressive satire” that exposes society’s wickedness by turning the dial on that wickedness up to 11. It’s a familiar argument, one that has been used frequently to justify artworks that explore humanity’s basest tendencies.

[Read: The right way to adapt a video game]

Many art genres—including some I like a great deal—use depictions of extreme violence as a form of social critique: gangster rap, death metal, horror movies, and so on. But a crucial difference between these works and a video game such as GTA 6 is that they do not require their audiences to reenact depravity. Gamers like to point out that violent video games do not seem to inspire players to enact real-world harm, and this is true. They also point out that many people who play games are productive members of society—good parents, partners, friends, and employees. This is also true. But surely “Does this product lead to real-world homicidal rage?” or “Does this activity sabotage most people’s personal lives?” are rather low bars to clear, and not the only metrics for evaluating whether something is worthwhile, let alone moral. If you had told H. G. Wells, or Aldous Huxley, or any of the great early-20th-century dystopian sci-fi writers that, in the 21st century, large segments of the adult population would spend much of their free time glued to a crime-and-murder simulator, they would have recognized what you are describing as a kind of dystopia.

What’s more, violence aside, GTA 6 is like every other video game in that it requires players to sit on their couch and give their undivided attention to the screen. I cannot kick the gut-level suspicion that has led me to keep my distance from video games throughout my adult life: Here is an island for lotus eating, one that invites you to waste away on its virtual soil. The fact that this particular game has high-minded aspirations, and maybe lives up to them, doesn’t mean that the lotus isn’t there waiting for you. Many modern video games, after all, have extensive, sophisticated design features that are purpose-built to keep players playing, and to disincentivize logging off, in a way that other immersive hobbies—including, say, reading novels, or bingeing television shows, or spending all of Sunday watching NFL games—do not.

With GTA 6, the medium remains the message, and the legitimate praise of this new game’s content seems to obscure the reality of its form: the controller, the couch, the screen, the hours in their grip. “I never want to leave,” PCMag’s Jordan Minor wrote. And isn’t that the very point and the very problem? GTA 6 cannot help but drain the distance between its critique of American life and much of what it criticizes. It satirizes the glorification of violence even as it offers violence as entertainment. It asks players to contemplate what it means to try to get your life together, even as droves of adults, here in the real world, take paid time off to play PlayStation. It asks men to consider what it means to be a good boyfriend, even as many of the men playing it are almost certainly neglecting their very real girlfriends and families and wives to do so. “Your bf is booking the day off work to do chores for his little game wife,” one woman joked on X. It’s a dark joke.

title: What Could Replace the Trump Style of Politics?
summary: Jonathan Spector’s play Birthright, which had a recent off-Broadway run, crescendos with what can best be described as a Google duel.
