content:
Jonathan Spector’s play Birthright, which had a recent off-Broadway run, crescendos with what can best be described as a Google duel. In the last act, which takes place in 2024, the nearly two-decade bond between a group of American Jewish friends has frayed over Gaza. Izzy, the most left-wing of the bunch, has already abandoned their online group chat, where the friends shared photos of their newborn children, checked in during COVID, and planned their reunions.

Thrown together for a funeral, Izzy and another friend, Chaya, begin to argue—as one does these days—about Zionism. They quickly whip out their phones, mustering evidence. “Theodor Herzl colonialism,” Izzy types into the search window, which—in an ingenious bit of stagecraft—appears projected on the wall behind her and starts to flow with online sources. “1930s partition plan Israel,” Chaya counter-Googles. They start scrolling through newspaper articles and Wikipedia pages, hurling raw historical information at each other like malfunctioning robots. But no one is listening. Their friend Noah, watching from the side, offers that going to the internet to prove your point is useless because you’ll invariably find what you’re looking for—“which is why I think this is really, really not a good way to go about having an actual conversation.”

This mode of political discourse is surely familiar: the search for a truth that will detonate like an atom bomb, ripping the roof off every other truth. Most of us know that this outcome never, ever happens. But beneath the awareness of information bubbles and fake news, of epistemic breakdown, lies a stubbornly common belief that total victory is achievable. This fantasy has even become its own kind of entertainment—think of Jubilee Media’s viral videos in which one person has to fend off 20 political opponents like a medieval knight, or the late Charlie Kirk’s “Prove Me Wrong” college tours. Theories are packed tight with facts and lobbed back and forth in what the German philosopher Hannah Arendt once called “an orgy of truth-telling.”

Arendt used this strange phrase in a 1946 letter to the philosopher Gershom Scholem, her dear intellectual sparring partner, after they had gotten into a fierce argument about—what else?—Zionism. One shouldn’t be a “fanatic for truth,” Arendt told him. All this did was harden people in their positions: I have my truth, you have yours, and the only way forward is for you to admit that not just your opinions but your facts are wrong. This is no way to hold a debate, or to conduct politics; all it does is create stasis or even worse. Elsewhere, Arendt called truth in this context “despotic.” She argued instead for a different mode, one that would be surprising—okay, maybe fantastical—to consider today: “an orgy of friendship.”

In a recently published book, A World We Share, Roger Berkowitz explores the German philosopher’s thoughts on friendship “as the lens through which she understood politics.” For Arendt, who is best known for her hard-bitten analysis of totalitarianism, friendship might seem to be an uncharacteristically schmaltzy subject, but as filtered through her mind, abstracted and held apart, it sheds all Hallmark associations. Berkowitz, the director of the Hannah Arendt Center for Politics and Humanities at Bard College, provides the material for an intriguing thought experiment, one that might be useful as Americans rub their eyes in the post-midterms dawn. After a decade in which Donald Trump’s tribalist instincts have only accelerated that rush to Google-dueling, it might be worth pursuing Arendt’s idea that friendship, as opposed to truth-telling, is a better model for conducting politics.

Arendt never left behind a treatise on friendship, but references to the concept pop up throughout her work and letters. Berkowitz, who has a granular familiarity with her writing, brings all of the strands together. For Arendt, friendship is distinct from love as we often think of it; it is not about losing yourself in order to meld with another person and separate from the rest of the world. Instead, this kind of connection preserves difference and feeds off plurality. Friendship is actually the most worldly of relationships because it forces us to accommodate the separateness of the people we know and care about.

[Read: It’s the morality, stupid]

Arendt articulated three defining features: time spent knowing each other (“a two-week-old friendship does not exist,” she said); talking and more talking and even more talking; and a respect and appreciation for the unique conditions that shape someone else’s worldview.

This kind of friendship, she thought, should withstand even the most violent disagreements. “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions,” she wrote in her letter to Scholem, begging that they not lose their connection despite her public disillusionment with the idea of an exclusively Jewish state—a critique Scholem must have felt as a body blow. Berkowitz points out that for Arendt, what makes us human “is not our ability to reason or our grasp of moral certainty or absolute truth but our ability to form lasting and meaningful relationships grounded in mutual recognition and respect.” The fact that she and Scholem had spent more than a decade talking, listening, and yelling was more important to her than any need for them to come to similar conclusions. Her emphasis was rather on this “in-between,” the “common world” they shared and built just by continuing to engage on the issues that mattered to them both.

Could any of this possibly be applicable to America’s political culture, which most days resembles the fear and loathing of trench warfare? Dream with me for a minute.

Imagine if arguments at Thanksgiving dinner or in Congress proceeded with an awareness that conquering the other person’s worldview was impossible—in the way you can’t really change that old friend who keeps dating the wrong people. Imagine if the goal was to tease out commonalities, instead of trying to will the differences away. This type of politics would be fueled by persuasion, as opposed to force or truth, Berkowitz writes; it would aim “neither at domination nor certainty. It is not about being right.”

Arendt’s favored metaphor for this in-between is a table around which people with disparate views and interests sit. The existence of the table matters more than anyone’s particular opinions. The American version of this table does exist, however alienated we may feel from one another. The changing state of the economy, for example, or the future of children’s education, are issues that could potentially be served at this table. Some topics—say, abortion rights—would produce more heat, maybe some fist-pounding. But if the objective is to make sure that the table itself doesn’t evaporate, the conversation might continue. Certain shared worries from our shared world will present themselves as commonalities, even as people’s perspectives remain distinct. Take the proliferation of data centers or the cost of health care. “By talking about what is between them,” Arendt writes, friends and citizens can make that shared world “ever more common.”

[Read: Why we should read Hannah Arendt now]

This is what an orgy of friendship (as opposed to one of truth) could look like. I don’t have any illusions that this shift of mindset is easy. But some politicians could point the way—for instance Senator-Elect James Talarico of Texas. “I really do believe that the key to saving the American experiment is loving our enemies,” he recently told Michelle Goldberg at The New York Times. “How do we love each other through our disagreements? How do we remember each other’s humanity? How do we handle each other with more care?” Talarico gives this a Christian gloss with his talk of “love,” which is not quite what Arendt had in mind, but she would otherwise be sympathetic to his willingness to make friends with those who have been calling him “Talafreako” for the past year. Of course, going to Washington could very well crush this friendliness out of him, but it is worth paying attention to how rhetorically effective his approach has been.

For anyone who might be rolling their eyes at the idea of friendship and politics occupying even the same sentence, I have two important caveats, both integral to Arendt’s thinking. First, Arendt was not some kind of postmodern relativist; she believed that truth exists and was deeply invested in it. Facts are what make a shared world possible in the first place; they are the floor on which that table stands. If her friendship metaphor seems implausible today, that might be because this basic prerequisite—that political actors agree on the contours of reality—often feels absent. Arendt’s answer to this problem would be to search outside politics for what she called the “truthtellers”—journalists and lawyers, scientists and artists, historians and philosophers. (I can only imagine the despair she’d feel at the idea that these backstops of democratic society are now often dismissed as out-of-touch elites.)

The second caveat is that friendship has its limits. Arendt was not suggesting that every disagreement can be overcome, or that preserving a relationship is always the highest good. Some people, and some ideas, are so destructive that they threaten the very possibility of living together. There is a difference between disagreeing about what the world should look like and refusing to recognize that other people have a place in it. Arendt understood this distinction well. She had barely gotten out of Nazi Germany alive.

After the war, she had to delineate these limits of friendship on a personal level: Should she reconnect with Germans who had allied with the Nazis? According to Berkowitz, she made an interesting rule for herself. Those who had acquiesced to the Nazis only in the early years, until the Nuremberg Laws were passed in 1935, but then recoiled from where Hitler was headed, she could reconcile with. They “were not all murderers,” she said. With these friends, she told a television interviewer in 1963, “it seemed to me that there should be a basis for communication precisely in the abyss of Auschwitz.” But when it came to those who continued supporting the party after Kristallnacht in 1938, when its genocidal intent became evident, there was no table to speak of.

The line is not always so obvious. Arendt’s own ambivalence over Martin Heidegger, her onetime mentor and lover, is revealing. Heidegger, the great philosopher, joined the Nazi Party and lent it his intellectual support; as the rector of his university, he even stripped his own mentor, Edmund Husserl, of his position there because he was Jewish. When exactly Heidegger stopped believing in the cause and started seeing it as “the greatest stupidity of my life,” as he later put it, is not clear. Arendt wouldn’t speak to him again until 1950, and she never publicly forgave him. But she did find a way to reconcile with him, and even renew their friendship. As Berkowitz put it, she decided that the world was better with Heidegger in it. This might seem at first like softness toward an old flame, but it wasn’t; her magnanimity looked like the result of disciplined reasoning. I’m not sure I could have ever spoken to him again, but I can respect that giving the benefit of the doubt seemed to be part of her ethic. This bears keeping in mind at a moment when a friend can be lost over whether he or she is willing to utter the word genocide.

[Read: What is Zionism?]

Arendt herself knew what it meant to be ostracized for one’s political positions. After the publication in 1963 of Eichmann in Jerusalem, her account of the trial of Adolf Eichmann, a key orchestrator of the Holocaust, she was roundly attacked—in part for describing Eichmann’s brand of evil as “banality,” but even more for the perception that she blamed the Jews for their own suffering and was insufficiently horrified by what befell them.

In her responses to the many incensed letters and calls for her excommunication, she repeatedly insists on friendship. This willingness to hold differences of opinion while maintaining a relationship even shows up in a novel about Arendt that was rereleased this month. In 1983, Arthur A. Cohen published An Admirable Woman, whose protagonist is an Arendt doppelgänger named Erika Hertz. She too is a German Jewish intellectual who escapes Nazism and becomes a celebrated thinker in New York. To add to the book’s hall-of-mirrors effect, at the very end we discover that Erika Hertz is actually friends with none other than Hannah Arendt. Hertz also takes issue with Eichmann in Jerusalem, but unlike so many others, she refuses to abandon Arendt over it.

“I think this is reckless,” Hertz says to herself about the book. And yet she also declares: “I will surely come to her aid.” The two judgments sit side by side. Neither cancels the other out. The point of friendship is not to confirm our view of the world. Hertz sees in Arendt a near copy of herself, and so she isn’t repulsed by this reminder of their separateness. Instead, it reinforces how much they need each other: “Rather than resemble, it is that we dissemble each other. My friend and I. I lie in the folds of her garments. She in mine.”

In real life, Arendt was deeply hurt by the friends who threatened to denounce and disavow her. Scholem, her old pen pal, was one of those who found himself on the cusp of saying goodbye to her forever. He judged that her account of the trial had betrayed a lack of ahavath Israel, “love of the Jewish people.” Arendt didn’t flinch. The warmth and connection that people could generate between themselves mattered to her above any other allegiance: “How right you are that I have no such love, and for two reasons: first, I have never in my life ‘loved’ any people or collective, neither the German nor the French nor the American, also not the working class or any other. I love in fact only my friends.”
